comparator.name: Art History
comparator.sourceNotes: The live 2026–27 Leiden Study Guide public product identifies two 180-EC formal routes, Arts and Culture and Arts, Media and Society. The generic registry target is represented by the broad historical Arts and Culture route, independently of UCR fit. Its current structure totals 60 EC in each year: compulsory first-year visual analysis, art and architecture history, world art and academic skills; a 40-EC compulsory second year with 10 EC of two selected 5-EC seminars and a selected 10-EC Florence excursion; and a third year with 10 EC compulsory research/publishing, one 10-EC BA3 seminar, a 10-EC Art History final paper and genuine 30-EC open elective space. The first-listed early/modern seminar pair and Florence excursion provide one coherent instantiation of formal restricted choices. The public product API supplies the official module identities and EC; its curriculum grouping supplies compulsory and choice status. The 2025–26 archived study guide warned of 2026–27 changes, so it was not used to carry forward superseded course weights or choices.

routeSelection.basis: The normalized target names generic Art History, not Arts, Media and Society. Leiden’s current official curriculum offers those two formal 180-EC routes. Arts and Culture spans the historical art and architecture periods, material study, museums, heritage, theory, methods and research that define the broad Art History identity; it is selected on that academic basis, before UCR course selection.

core: European art history from antiquity through the early modern and modern periods, with analysis of painting, sculpture and architecture
Material culture, architectural form and the making of objects
Global and cross-regional art history, including Africa and the Americas
Museums, collecting, display, cultural heritage and the interpretation of artworks
Visual analysis, art-historical methods, evidence-based interpretation and the historiography of art
Historical and social contexts of art and culture across periods
Art-historical seminars, research and independent final paper
adjacent: Contemporary art, media and society as an official alternative within Leiden Art History, connecting visual culture, digital media and social questions
Communication, representation and cultural meaning in modern visual and audiovisual media
questions: How do museums and heritage institutions select, display and interpret art?
How do contemporary images, media and artistic practices shape public understanding of society and global issues?

courses: New Issues in Contemporary Social Theory
trace: Provides the modern-period historical context needed to situate nineteenth- and twentieth-century art in social and political change.
Examines imperial histories and colonial relations that shape the cross-regional circulation and interpretation of art and heritage.
Studies Native American histories and cultural expressions, providing a specific historical context for art and heritage in the Americas.
Trains independent source-based historical research and argumentation; the course topic is history rather than art, so it supplements art-historical research methods.
Studies ethical reasoning that can be applied to ownership, presentation and contested heritage; it is a complementary method, not a museum-studies substitute.
Introduces sociological theories of how cultural production and media relate to social structures.
Teaches qualitative research design and interpretation useful for studying audiences, institutions and cultural meaning.
Studies colonialism, modernity and social theory as frames for contemporary visual culture and cultural representation.
Examines contemporary social theory and civil society, giving conceptual grounding for socially engaged art and media.
Studies rhetorical interpretation of visual and public discourse, including advertising and public messages.
Studies how stylistic choices produce meaning in texts, a specific analytic complement to media representation.
Directly analyzes films, exhibitions, protest art and social media in public debate about climate change.
Studies persuasion across communication and society, complementing analysis of how contemporary visual culture addresses publics.
Studies and creates artistic communication through theory, performance and reflective writing.
Surveys Western art from the Renaissance onward and interprets painting, artistic movements and art institutions.
Studies the making, materiality and interpretation of objects across world regions, complementing art history with archaeological evidence.
Examines African artistic traditions and heritage, extending the historical art curriculum beyond Europe.
Directly examines Renaissance painting, sculpture and architecture through Mediterranean trade and cross-cultural exchange.
Uses Greek archaeology and material evidence to investigate ancient community life, a specific ancient material-culture complement rather than a survey of ancient art.
Directly studies modern art and the curatorial and exhibition choices of modern museums.
Investigates the political meanings of ancient heritage and civic memory, a specific complement to heritage interpretation rather than architectural history.
Studies the history, theorists and methods of art history, including visual analysis and art-historical writing.
Studies major literary sources and their enduring relation to Western visual arts and cultural themes; this supplies iconographic context, not art-history instruction.
Examines global myths and narratives that furnish identifiable subjects and interpretive contexts for historical art.
Studies film adaptation from literary texts, connecting cinematic visual form to stories and cultural interpretation.
Introduces film history, visual analysis and the development of film as cultural expression.
Studies physical media technologies and their role in cultural production and preservation, adding a material-media perspective to visual culture.
Examines the social history of television and contemporary mainstream media, focusing on who produces and frames public narratives.
Analyzes visual and audiovisual representations of environmental issues, including Indigenous and postcolonial media.
Examines how film, photographs and music represent race, memory, power and resistance.
Analyzes the history and visual techniques of documentary film as an artistic and social representation form.

alternatives.label: Art, Heritage and Historical Cultures
alternatives.labelReason: The curriculum has eight art/archaeology/heritage courses, dedicated modern museum and art-historiography courses, visual media, source-based historical research and specific historical, literary and ethical complements. It follows the broad historic Arts and Culture route while acknowledging that UCR offers fewer art-specific courses and no equivalent thesis.
alternatives.concept: A historical art and material-culture programme centred on UCR’s art-history, archaeology, museum and heritage courses, with history, literature and visual-media study supplying specific contexts for objects and their interpretation across periods and regions.
progression: All formal prerequisites and Fall-2026-cohort semester offerings were checked against the current enriched workbook. PPD is in the first semester. Introduction to Western Art History precedes the later art-history courses; material culture, historical survey and media foundations generally precede advanced art, museum and research work.

alternatives.label: Contemporary Art, Media and Society
alternatives.labelReason: The final 24-course programme combines six UCR art/heritage courses with six media courses, five communication courses, four sociology courses, film and ethics. Its centre of gravity is contemporary visual representation and social meaning, a distinct response to Leiden’s official Arts, Media and Society direction.
alternatives.concept: A contemporary visual-culture route that studies how art, film, exhibitions, digital media and communication shape social meaning, public debate and representation. It retains an art-historical base but gives substantially more weight to media and social theory than the historical Arts and Culture response.
alternatives.distinctness: Eight courses (60 EC) differ in each direction: this route replaces historical, archaeological and literary contexts with television/social media, environment, film adaptation, communication and sociology. The change follows Leiden’s formally documented Arts, Media and Society direction and alters the academic centre of the 24-course curriculum.
progression: All formal prerequisites and planned semester offerings were checked against the current enriched workbook. PPD is in Year 1. Introductory art history, media and sociology are scheduled before advanced art history, media, communication and social-theory work where the offerings permit.

selection.assessment: The closest programme substantively covers all nine generator-eligible art-history, visual-object, architecture, heritage and historical-culture interests (rows 13552–13560). The remaining generator-eligible row 13561 and the current official Arts, Media and Society route support a coherent second programme with a distinct media/social-theory curriculum; its course sets differ by eight courses (60 EC) each way and both schedules satisfy the hard constraints. No further generator-eligible interest or independently evidenced third organising direction remains. Production therefore stops at two.

notes.text: Leiden’s Arts and Culture route gives sustained art-historical work across visual analysis, material techniques, architecture, several periods of European and world art, museums, heritage, aesthetics, specialised seminars and an Art History final paper. UCR offers a smaller art-history and heritage sequence and adds relevant history, archaeology, media and cultural-analysis courses; it does not reproduce the full specialist sequence or dedicated final paper.
